answers.question: What is TransactionTemplate and how does programmatic transaction management work? Explain execute vs executeWithoutResult, how it compares to @Transactional, and how it fixes the self-invocation problem.
answers.shortTitle: TransactionTemplate — programmatic transaction management

s1_definition.profdef: `TransactionTemplate` is a Spring helper class that lets you manage transactions in your own code instead of relying on the `@Transactional` annotation. You wrap the code that must run inside a transaction in a callback, and the template takes care of starting the transaction before the callback runs, committing it if the callback finishes normally, and rolling it back if the callback throws a runtime exception. It wraps a `PlatformTransactionManager` and gives you fine-grained, line-by-line control over exactly which statements are inside the transaction.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India. With `@Transactional`, Rajesh hands his whole form to a clerk and says "do everything or nothing." With `TransactionTemplate`, Rajesh himself stands at the counter, says "open the ledger now" (begin), writes exactly the two lines he wants (debit his savings, credit Priya), and then says "close and stamp the ledger" (commit). If anything looks wrong mid-way, he tears up the page (rollback). He controls the exact start and end point of the transaction himself.
s1_definition.oneliner: `TransactionTemplate` is you driving the transaction manually — begin, run your code, commit or rollback — instead of letting the annotation drive for you.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `TransactionTemplate` is a Spring helper class that lets you manage transactions in your own code instead of relying on the `@Transactional` annotation. You wrap the code that must run inside a transaction in a callback, and the template takes care of starting the transaction before the callback runs, committing it if the callback finishes normally, and rolling it back if the callback throws a runtime exception. It wraps a `PlatformTransactionManager` and gives you fine-grained, line-by-line control over exactly which statements are inside the transaction.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India. With `@Transactional`, Rajesh hands his whole form to a clerk and says "do everything or nothing." With `TransactionTemplate`, Rajesh himself stands at the counter, says "open the ledger now" (begin), writes exactly the two lines he wants (debit his savings, credit Priya), and then says "close and stamp the ledger" (commit). If anything looks wrong mid-way, he tears up the page (rollback). He controls the exact start and end point of the transaction himself.

**One line to remember:** `TransactionTemplate` is you driving the transaction manually — begin, run your code, commit or rollback — instead of letting the annotation drive for you.

sections.s2_technical:
A `TransactionTemplate` is created from a `PlatformTransactionManager`. In Spring Boot the transaction manager is auto-configured, so you just inject it and build the template once: `new TransactionTemplate(txManager)`. The template is thread-safe once configured, so you can create it once and reuse it.

The main method is `execute`. It takes a `TransactionCallback<T>` and returns a value. For example, if you want to transfer money and return the new balance, you write `BigDecimal newBalance = txTemplate.execute(status -> { rajesh.debit(amount); priya.credit(amount); return rajesh.getBalance(); });`. The template begins a transaction, runs your lambda, and commits automatically when the lambda returns. If the lambda throws a `RuntimeException`, the template rolls back and re-throws.

When your code does not need to return anything, use `executeWithoutResult`. It takes a `Consumer<TransactionStatus>` instead of a function. For example `txTemplate.executeWithoutResult(status -> { rajesh.debit(amount); priya.credit(amount); });`. This is cleaner than `execute` with a `return null;` at the end. It was added in Spring 5.2 specifically so you do not have to return a dummy value.

The `TransactionStatus` object passed into the callback is powerful. You can call `status.setRollbackOnly()` to force a rollback without throwing an exception — useful when a business rule fails but you do not want to throw. For example `if (rajesh.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0) { status.setRollbackOnly(); return; }`.

You can configure the template just like the annotation attributes. `txTemplate.setPropagationBehavior(TransactionDefinition.PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW)` sets propagation, `txTemplate.setIsolationLevel(TransactionDefinition.ISOLATION_READ_COMMITTED)` sets isolation, `txTemplate.setTimeout(5)` sets a five second timeout, and `txTemplate.setReadOnly(true)` marks it read-only.

Compared to `@Transactional`, the annotation is declarative and clean but it works through an AOP proxy, so it only applies when the method is called from outside the bean. `TransactionTemplate` is programmatic — the transaction boundary is the lambda, decided at runtime by actual method calls, so there is no proxy involved.

This is exactly why `TransactionTemplate` fixes the self-invocation problem. With `@Transactional`, if method `a()` in a bean calls `this.b()` where `b()` is annotated, the annotation on `b()` is ignored because the call does not go through the proxy — it is a plain `this` call. With `TransactionTemplate` there is no proxy, so you can start a transaction from any private helper method, even one called internally, and it always works. A senior developer reaches for `TransactionTemplate` when they need a transaction around a small block inside a larger method, or inside a method that is called internally, or when they need to react to the `TransactionStatus` mid-flight.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, there is a batch job that processes a list of pending transfers overnight. Each transfer must be its own independent transaction, because if transfer number three fails, transfers one and two should still be saved. If we put `@Transactional` on the whole batch method, one failure rolls back the entire batch. This is exactly what programmatic transaction management with `PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW` solves — we wrap each single transfer in its own `TransactionTemplate.executeWithoutResult` call so each commits or rolls back on its own.

Problem 2 — The batch method and the single-transfer logic live in the same service class. The batch method calls the transfer method internally using `this`. If the transfer method relied on `@Transactional`, the annotation would be silently ignored because of self-invocation — the call never goes through the Spring proxy. This is exactly why we use `TransactionTemplate` inside the internal method: it starts a real transaction regardless of how the method was called.

Problem 3 — Sometimes a transfer should be quietly skipped when Rajesh does not have enough balance, without throwing a loud exception that pollutes the logs. This is exactly what `status.setRollbackOnly()` is for — we mark the transaction for rollback and return cleanly.

What the code will do. The `Account` class holds accountId, holderName, and balance with `debit` and `credit` methods. The `AccountRepository` loads and saves accounts. The `TransferService` holds a `TransactionTemplate` built from the injected `PlatformTransactionManager`. Its `runBatch` method loops over a list of transfers and calls the internal `transferOne` method for each. The `transferOne` method uses `executeWithoutResult` with `REQUIRES_NEW` so each transfer is its own transaction, uses `setRollbackOnly` when the balance is too low, and demonstrates that self-invocation still gets a real transaction. The demo wires everything, runs a batch of three transfers where the middle one fails, and shows that the other two still commit.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a batch of three transfers. Transfer one is SAV2001 to CUR3001 for Rs.50,000. Transfer two is CUR3001 to SAV2001 for Rs.9,999,999 which is far more than Priya's balance. Transfer three is SAV2001 to CUR3001 for Rs.25,000.

Step 1. The `runBatch` method starts. It is NOT inside any transaction yet. It loops and calls `transferOne` for the first request. This is a self-invocation using `this`.

Step 2. Inside `transferOne`, the `TransactionTemplate` begins a fresh REQUIRES_NEW transaction. Rajesh's balance is Rs.1,000,000 which is enough for Rs.50,000. The debit and credit happen, both accounts are saved, and the lambda returns normally, so the template commits. Rajesh is now at Rs.950,000 and Priya at Rs.300,000.

Step 3. The loop calls `transferOne` for the second request. A new transaction begins. Priya's balance is only Rs.300,000 which is less than Rs.9,999,999. The code calls `status.setRollbackOnly()` and returns. The template sees the rollback-only flag and rolls back. No exception is thrown, no money moves, and the loop continues normally.

Step 4. The loop calls `transferOne` for the third request. A new transaction begins. Rajesh has Rs.950,000 which is enough for Rs.25,000. The debit and credit happen and the template commits. Rajesh is now at Rs.925,000 and Priya at Rs.325,000.

Step 5. The batch finishes. Two transfers committed, one rolled back cleanly, and each was fully independent because of REQUIRES_NEW.

sections.s6_takeaway:
TransactionTemplate is Spring's way of doing programmatic transaction management. Instead of putting the Transactional annotation on a method and letting the AOP proxy start and end the transaction, I build a TransactionTemplate from the PlatformTransactionManager and wrap the code I want inside a callback. The template begins the transaction before my callback runs, commits it when the callback returns normally, and rolls it back if the callback throws a runtime exception. I use the execute method when I need to return a value, and executeWithoutResult when I do not, which avoids the ugly return null at the end.

In my banking project we had an overnight batch job that processed many pending transfers. We deliberately did not make the batch method transactional, because if one transfer failed we did not want to lose all the others. Instead, each single transfer ran inside its own TransactionTemplate call configured with REQUIRES_NEW propagation, so every transfer committed or rolled back completely independently. When Rajesh had insufficient balance we called setRollbackOnly on the TransactionStatus to roll back cleanly without throwing a loud exception.

The most important reason I reach for TransactionTemplate is the self-invocation problem. With the Transactional annotation, if a method in a bean calls another annotated method on the same bean using this, the annotation is silently ignored because the call never passes through the Spring proxy. Since TransactionTemplate is programmatic and does not rely on a proxy at all, I can start a real transaction from any internal helper method and it always works.

So the way I summarize it in an interview is that the annotation is declarative and clean for the common case, but TransactionTemplate gives me explicit, line-by-line control over the transaction boundary, lets me react to the transaction status mid-flight, makes each item in a batch independent, and sidesteps the self-invocation trap entirely. I choose it whenever I need a transaction around a small block, inside an internally-called method, or when the boundaries must be decided at runtime.

answers.question: What does @Transactional(readOnly = true) do? Explain how it sets the Hibernate flush mode to MANUAL, skips dirty-checking, and can route to a read replica. Is read-only a guarantee or only a hint?
answers.shortTitle: @Transactional(readOnly = true) — what it really does

s1_definition.profdef: `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` marks a transaction as read-only, which tells the persistence layer that no data will be modified. For Hibernate this sets the flush mode to MANUAL so the session does not automatically flush changes, and it skips the expensive dirty-checking that normally compares every loaded entity against its original snapshot at flush time. It also acts as a hint that routing infrastructure can use to send queries to a read replica. Importantly, read-only is a hint and an optimization, not a hard guarantee enforced by the database.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh goes to the National Bank of India just to check his balance and download a statement. He is not changing anything, only reading. If we tell the clerk "this is a read-only visit," the clerk does not bother re-checking every ledger page for edits before Rajesh leaves (that is skipping dirty-checking), and the bank can send Rajesh to the fast "enquiry only" counter instead of the busy "transactions" counter (that is read replica routing). But the clerk is trusting Rajesh — if Rajesh somehow scribbles on a page, the system may not stop him, because read-only is a polite instruction, not a locked vault.
s1_definition.oneliner: `readOnly = true` makes read transactions faster by turning off dirty-checking and auto-flush and hinting replica routing, but it optimizes rather than strictly forbidding writes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` marks a transaction as read-only, which tells the persistence layer that no data will be modified. For Hibernate this sets the flush mode to MANUAL so the session does not automatically flush changes, and it skips the expensive dirty-checking that normally compares every loaded entity against its original snapshot at flush time. It also acts as a hint that routing infrastructure can use to send queries to a read replica. Importantly, read-only is a hint and an optimization, not a hard guarantee enforced by the database.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh goes to the National Bank of India just to check his balance and download a statement. He is not changing anything, only reading. If we tell the clerk "this is a read-only visit," the clerk does not bother re-checking every ledger page for edits before Rajesh leaves (that is skipping dirty-checking), and the bank can send Rajesh to the fast "enquiry only" counter instead of the busy "transactions" counter (that is read replica routing). But the clerk is trusting Rajesh — if Rajesh somehow scribbles on a page, the system may not stop him, because read-only is a polite instruction, not a locked vault.

**One line to remember:** `readOnly = true` makes read transactions faster by turning off dirty-checking and auto-flush and hinting replica routing, but it optimizes rather than strictly forbidding writes.

sections.s2_technical:
When you write `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` on a service method, Spring sets the `readOnly` flag on the transaction definition. Spring then passes this flag down to the underlying resource. For a Hibernate or JPA setup, Spring sets the Hibernate `Session` flush mode to `FlushMode.MANUAL`. For example a balance enquiry method would look like `@Transactional(readOnly = true) public BigDecimal getBalance(String accountId) { return accountRepo.findById(accountId).getBalance(); }`.

With flush mode MANUAL, Hibernate will not automatically flush pending changes before queries or at commit. In a normal read-write transaction the flush mode is AUTO, which means Hibernate flushes dirty entities to the database before each query and at commit. Turning this off saves work because there is nothing to write.

The second big optimization is skipping dirty-checking. Normally, when you load an entity, Hibernate keeps a snapshot of its original field values. At flush time it compares the current values against the snapshot to decide what UPDATE statements to generate. In a read-only transaction Hibernate can skip taking and comparing these snapshots, which saves both CPU and memory, especially when you load thousands of rows for a report. For example, generating Priya's annual statement might load ten thousand transaction rows; with read-only, Hibernate does not waste memory holding a snapshot of each one.

The third benefit is read replica routing. Many production systems use an `AbstractRoutingDataSource` that picks the data source based on the current transaction's read-only flag. Spring exposes whether the current transaction is read-only through `TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly()`. A custom routing data source reads this flag and returns the replica connection when it is true and the primary connection when it is false. For example `protected Object determineCurrentLookupKey() { return TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly() ? "REPLICA" : "PRIMARY"; }`. This spreads heavy read traffic like reports and statements onto replicas and keeps the primary free for writes.

Now the crucial senior-level nuance: read-only is a hint, not a guarantee. At the JDBC level Spring calls `connection.setReadOnly(true)`, but the JDBC spec says this is only a hint to the driver for optimization, and many drivers ignore it. Nothing physically stops a SQL UPDATE from running on most databases unless the database itself enforces it, for example when you are actually connected to a true physical read replica that rejects writes. With Hibernate, if you do modify an entity inside a read-only transaction, Hibernate will usually not flush the change because flush mode is MANUAL, so the write silently does nothing rather than throwing an error. That silent no-op is exactly why junior developers get confused when a "save" inside a read-only method appears to do nothing.

A few more practical notes. Read-only transactions still have all the propagation and isolation behavior of normal transactions, so you still get a consistent snapshot of the data for the duration of the method. You should put `readOnly = true` on query and report methods, and leave it off (default false) on anything that writes. Mixing a write into a read-only method is a bug. A common pattern is a service where query methods are read-only and command methods are read-write, which also makes replica routing automatic and correct.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the reporting team runs heavy queries all day: account statements, transaction histories, portfolio summaries. These queries loaded thousands of rows and the primary database was getting hammered, slowing down actual money transfers for customers like Rajesh and Priya. This is exactly what read replica routing with `readOnly = true` solves — read queries go to a replica and the primary stays free for writes.

Problem 2 — When generating Priya's annual statement, Hibernate loaded ten thousand transaction rows and kept a dirty-checking snapshot of each one, wasting memory and CPU comparing them at commit even though nothing changed. This is exactly what skipping dirty-checking in a read-only transaction fixes — no snapshots, no comparison, lower memory.

Problem 3 — A junior developer accidentally called `account.setBalance(...)` inside a read-only statement method and was confused that the balance never updated in the database. This is exactly the hint-not-guarantee behavior — flush mode MANUAL meant Hibernate never flushed the change, so it silently did nothing. Understanding this prevents a whole class of confusing bugs.

What the code will do. The `Account` class holds accountId, holderName, and balance. The `AccountRepository` loads accounts. A `RoutingDataSource` decides PRIMARY versus REPLICA based on the read-only flag. The `StatementService` has a read-only `getBalance` method and a read-only `generateStatement` method, plus a read-write `transfer` method to contrast. The demo shows a read-only call routing to the replica with dirty-checking skipped, and shows that a stray write inside the read-only method silently does nothing, while the real transfer on the read-write path does update.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a balance enquiry for SAV2001 (read-only), then a transfer of Rs.50,000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 (read-write).

Step 1. The `getBalance` method is marked read-only. Spring sets the transaction definition's read-only flag to true and sets the Hibernate flush mode to MANUAL.

Step 2. The routing data source checks the read-only flag, sees it is true, and returns the REPLICA connection. The query to read Rajesh's balance runs on the replica, keeping the primary free.

Step 3. Hibernate loads Rajesh's account. Because the transaction is read-only, Hibernate skips taking a dirty-checking snapshot, saving memory.

Step 4. The code accidentally calls `setBalance(999)` on the loaded account. Because flush mode is MANUAL, Hibernate never flushes this change. At commit, nothing is written. The stray write silently does nothing — this is the hint-not-guarantee behavior.

Step 5. The method returns the real stored balance, Rs.1,000,000. The database still holds Rs.1,000,000.

Step 6. The `transfer` method runs. It is read-write (default). The routing data source sees read-only is false and returns the PRIMARY connection. Rajesh is debited Rs.50,000 and Priya credited Rs.50,000. Flush mode is AUTO, so the changes flush and commit. Rajesh is now Rs.950,000 and Priya Rs.300,000.

```

2026-10-23 15:50:01 [INFO   ] Rajesh balance read = 1000000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The readOnly equals true attribute on the Transactional annotation tells Spring and the persistence layer that this transaction will only read data and will not modify anything. For Hibernate, Spring uses this flag to set the flush mode to MANUAL, which means Hibernate will not automatically flush changes before queries or at commit, and it also lets Hibernate skip the dirty-checking snapshots it normally keeps for every loaded entity. That saves a lot of CPU and memory when a report loads thousands of rows.

In my banking project the reporting queries were hammering the primary database and slowing down real customer transfers. We used an AbstractRoutingDataSource that checks TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly and returns the read replica connection when the transaction is read-only and the primary connection when it is not. So just by marking our query methods as read-only, all the heavy statement and history queries automatically went to the replica and kept the primary free for writes like Rajesh transferring money to Priya.

The nuance I always mention is that read-only is a hint, not a guarantee. At the JDBC level Spring calls setReadOnly on the connection, but the spec says drivers may ignore it, so nothing physically blocks a write on most databases unless you are actually connected to a true physical replica. With Hibernate, if you accidentally modify an entity inside a read-only method, the change usually just does not get flushed because the flush mode is MANUAL, so it silently does nothing. That silent no-op confuses a lot of junior developers who expect either a save or an error.

So my rule in practice is simple. I put readOnly equals true on every query and report method and leave it off on anything that writes. This makes the code faster, makes replica routing automatic and correct, and clearly documents intent. But I never rely on it as a safety mechanism to prevent writes, because it is an optimization and a hint, not an enforced lock.

answers.question: What is @TransactionalEventListener? Explain the BEFORE_COMMIT, AFTER_COMMIT, and AFTER_ROLLBACK phases, how it differs from @EventListener, and what fallbackExecution does.
answers.shortTitle: @TransactionalEventListener — commit-aware event handling

s1_definition.profdef: `@TransactionalEventListener` is a Spring annotation that lets an event handler run at a specific phase of the surrounding transaction's lifecycle rather than immediately when the event is published. You choose the phase with the `phase` attribute: `BEFORE_COMMIT` runs just before the transaction commits, `AFTER_COMMIT` runs only after a successful commit, `AFTER_ROLLBACK` runs only if the transaction rolled back, and `AFTER_COMPLETION` runs after either outcome. It differs from the plain `@EventListener`, which runs synchronously the instant the event is published, regardless of whether the transaction later commits or rolls back.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh transfers money to Priya at the National Bank of India, the bank publishes an internal note that says "transfer happened." With a plain `@EventListener`, the SMS team sends Rajesh a success text the moment the note is written, even if the transfer later fails and gets reversed — that is a lie. With `@TransactionalEventListener` set to AFTER_COMMIT, the SMS team waits until the ledger is actually stamped and final before sending the text, so the customer never gets a false confirmation. BEFORE_COMMIT lets a fraud team do one last check while the ink is still wet, and AFTER_ROLLBACK lets a team log that the transfer was reversed.
s1_definition.oneliner: `@TransactionalEventListener` ties your handler to the transaction outcome, so side effects like SMS or emails only fire when the transaction truly commits.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@TransactionalEventListener` is a Spring annotation that lets an event handler run at a specific phase of the surrounding transaction's lifecycle rather than immediately when the event is published. You choose the phase with the `phase` attribute: `BEFORE_COMMIT` runs just before the transaction commits, `AFTER_COMMIT` runs only after a successful commit, `AFTER_ROLLBACK` runs only if the transaction rolled back, and `AFTER_COMPLETION` runs after either outcome. It differs from the plain `@EventListener`, which runs synchronously the instant the event is published, regardless of whether the transaction later commits or rolls back.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh transfers money to Priya at the National Bank of India, the bank publishes an internal note that says "transfer happened." With a plain `@EventListener`, the SMS team sends Rajesh a success text the moment the note is written, even if the transfer later fails and gets reversed — that is a lie. With `@TransactionalEventListener` set to AFTER_COMMIT, the SMS team waits until the ledger is actually stamped and final before sending the text, so the customer never gets a false confirmation. BEFORE_COMMIT lets a fraud team do one last check while the ink is still wet, and AFTER_ROLLBACK lets a team log that the transfer was reversed.

**One line to remember:** `@TransactionalEventListener` ties your handler to the transaction outcome, so side effects like SMS or emails only fire when the transaction truly commits.

sections.s2_technical:
You publish an event using Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher`, typically from inside a transactional service method. For example `eventPublisher.publishEvent(new TransferCompletedEvent("SAV2001", "CUR3001", amount));`. A listener method annotated with `@TransactionalEventListener` then receives it, but only at the chosen transaction phase.

The `AFTER_COMMIT` phase is the most common and the safest for external side effects. The handler runs only after the transaction has successfully committed, so you know the data is durable. For example `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT) public void sendSms(TransferCompletedEvent e) { smsGateway.send(e.getFrom(), "Transfer of Rs." + e.getAmount() + " successful"); }`. This guarantees you never send a success SMS for a transfer that actually rolled back.

The `BEFORE_COMMIT` phase runs just before the commit while the transaction is still open. Work done here still participates in the same transaction, so if this handler throws, the transaction rolls back. For example you might flush a final audit row: `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.BEFORE_COMMIT) public void finalAudit(TransferCompletedEvent e) { auditRepo.save(new AuditRow(e)); }`. Because it is before commit, that audit row is committed atomically with the transfer.

The `AFTER_ROLLBACK` phase runs only when the transaction rolled back. This is where you log failures or trigger compensation. For example `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_ROLLBACK) public void onFailure(TransferCompletedEvent e) { log.severe("Transfer rolled back: " + e.getFrom()); }`. There is also `AFTER_COMPLETION`, which runs after the transaction ends either way, useful for cleanup that must happen regardless of outcome.

The key difference from `@EventListener` is timing and coupling to the transaction. A plain `@EventListener` runs synchronously the moment `publishEvent` is called, inside the same thread and still inside the open transaction. That means if you send an SMS from a plain listener and the transaction later rolls back, the SMS was already sent — a false confirmation. `@TransactionalEventListener` solves exactly this by deferring the handler to a transaction phase.

A critical gotcha is the `fallbackExecution` attribute. By default, if a `@TransactionalEventListener` receives an event but there is no active transaction, the handler is simply not executed at all — it is silently dropped. This surprises developers who publish an event from a non-transactional method and wonder why their SMS never sent. Setting `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT, fallbackExecution = true)` tells Spring to run the handler immediately when there is no transaction, as a fallback. For example this is useful for a notification listener that should work whether or not the caller wrapped things in a transaction.

A few senior-level nuances. First, by default the AFTER_COMMIT handler runs on the same thread after commit, so a slow SMS call blocks the request thread; combine it with `@Async` to run it on a separate thread. Second, writing to the database inside an AFTER_COMMIT handler is tricky because the original transaction is already finished, so you typically need a new transaction with `REQUIRES_NEW` there. Third, BEFORE_COMMIT is the right place for last-minute database work that must be atomic with the main transaction, while AFTER_COMMIT is the right place for external systems like SMS, email, Kafka, and webhooks where you must be sure the data really committed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — When Rajesh transfers money to Priya, the National Bank of India must send an SMS confirmation. Early on, the SMS was sent from a plain event listener the instant the transfer method published the event. But sometimes the transfer failed validation after that point and rolled back, yet Rajesh had already received a "transfer successful" SMS. Customers complained about false confirmations. This is exactly what `@TransactionalEventListener` with AFTER_COMMIT fixes — the SMS fires only after the commit truly succeeds.

Problem 2 — The compliance team needs a final audit record written atomically with every transfer, so the audit and the money movement commit together or not at all. This is exactly what the BEFORE_COMMIT phase provides — the handler runs while the transaction is still open, so the audit row is part of the same commit.

Problem 3 — When a transfer rolls back, the operations team wants a clear failure log and a reversal notice. This is exactly what the AFTER_ROLLBACK phase does — the handler runs only on rollback.

Problem 4 — A separate internal tool published the same event from a non-transactional utility method, and the SMS mysteriously never sent. This is exactly the default fallbackExecution behavior — with no active transaction the handler is dropped. Setting fallbackExecution to true makes it run anyway.

What the code will do. The `Account` class holds balance with debit and credit. The `TransferCompletedEvent` carries from, to, and amount. The `TransferService` is transactional, moves the money, and publishes the event. Three listeners demonstrate BEFORE_COMMIT (final audit), AFTER_COMMIT (SMS, with fallbackExecution), and AFTER_ROLLBACK (failure log). The demo runs one successful transfer and one failing transfer and shows which listeners fire in each case.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a successful transfer of Rs.50,000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001, then a failing transfer of Rs.9,999,999 from CUR3001 to SAV2001.

Step 1. The successful transfer begins inside a transaction. Rajesh has enough balance. The debit and credit happen and both accounts are saved.

Step 2. The BEFORE_COMMIT listener fires while the transaction is still open. It saves the audit row. Because this is before the commit, the audit row and the money movement will commit together atomically.

Step 3. The transaction commits. The data is now durable.

Step 4. The AFTER_COMMIT listener fires. It sends Rajesh an SMS saying the transfer of Rs.50,000 was successful. This is safe because the commit already happened.

Step 5. The failing transfer begins. Priya does not have Rs.9,999,999. The code throws an exception before any save completes meaningfully, and the transaction rolls back.

Step 6. The AFTER_ROLLBACK listener fires. It logs the failure and notifies operations. The AFTER_COMMIT SMS listener does NOT fire, so Rajesh never gets a false success SMS.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The TransactionalEventListener annotation lets an event handler run at a specific phase of the surrounding transaction instead of immediately when the event is published. I choose the phase with the phase attribute. BEFORE_COMMIT runs just before commit and still participates in the same transaction, so work done there is atomic with the main operation. In my banking project we originally sent the transfer confirmation SMS from a plain listener, and sometimes the transfer rolled back after the event was published, so Rajesh received a success SMS for a transfer that never actually happened. We moved the SMS listener to AFTER_COMMIT, and from then on the SMS only fired when the transfer was truly committed and durable, which eliminated false confirmations completely.

We used the phases deliberately. The compliance audit row was written in a BEFORE_COMMIT listener so it committed atomically with the money movement. The SMS and email went in an AFTER_COMMIT listener. The failure logging and operations alert went in an AFTER_ROLLBACK listener. We also marked the AFTER_COMMIT listener with Async so a slow SMS gateway would not block the customer's request thread.

The one gotcha I always call out is fallbackExecution. By default, if the event is published when there is no active transaction, the handler is silently dropped and nothing happens, which confuses people. Setting fallbackExecution to true tells Spring to run the handler immediately when there is no transaction. So in interviews I summarize it as: use AFTER_COMMIT for anything that talks to the outside world so you never lie to the customer, use BEFORE_COMMIT for last-minute work that must be atomic, use AFTER_ROLLBACK for failure handling, and remember that without an active transaction the handler is dropped unless you enable fallback execution.

answers.question: What are distributed transactions using JTA and XA with two-phase commit? Why are they discouraged in microservices, and what are the alternatives like Saga, the Outbox pattern, and eventual consistency?
answers.shortTitle: Distributed transactions — JTA/XA 2PC and why Saga is preferred

s1_definition.profdef: A distributed transaction spans more than one resource, such as two databases or a database and a message broker, and must commit or roll back all of them atomically. The classic mechanism is JTA (the Java Transaction API) coordinating XA-compliant resources using two-phase commit. In phase one, a coordinator asks every resource to prepare and vote; in phase two, if all voted yes, it tells them all to commit, otherwise all to roll back. In microservices this is discouraged because it couples services tightly, holds locks across network calls, scales poorly, and the coordinator is a single point of failure. The common alternatives are the Saga pattern, the transactional Outbox pattern, and designing for eventual consistency.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must move money and, at the same instant, update a separate insurance system. Two-phase commit is like a wedding officiant asking both the bride and groom "do you agree?" and only finalizing the marriage if both say yes. The problem is everyone must stand frozen at the altar holding their breath (holding locks) while the officiant waits for slow replies over the phone. If the officiant faints mid-ceremony (coordinator crash), everyone is stuck. In microservices we instead do the steps one at a time and, if a later step fails, we run a "sorry, undo that" step — that is Saga.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two-phase commit gives strict atomicity across resources but holds locks across the network and needs a coordinator, so microservices prefer Saga plus Outbox with eventual consistency.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A distributed transaction spans more than one resource, such as two databases or a database and a message broker, and must commit or roll back all of them atomically. The classic mechanism is JTA (the Java Transaction API) coordinating XA-compliant resources using two-phase commit. In phase one, a coordinator asks every resource to prepare and vote; in phase two, if all voted yes, it tells them all to commit, otherwise all to roll back. In microservices this is discouraged because it couples services tightly, holds locks across network calls, scales poorly, and the coordinator is a single point of failure. The common alternatives are the Saga pattern, the transactional Outbox pattern, and designing for eventual consistency.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India must move money and, at the same instant, update a separate insurance system. Two-phase commit is like a wedding officiant asking both the bride and groom "do you agree?" and only finalizing the marriage if both say yes. The problem is everyone must stand frozen at the altar holding their breath (holding locks) while the officiant waits for slow replies over the phone. If the officiant faints mid-ceremony (coordinator crash), everyone is stuck. In microservices we instead do the steps one at a time and, if a later step fails, we run a "sorry, undo that" step — that is Saga.

**One line to remember:** Two-phase commit gives strict atomicity across resources but holds locks across the network and needs a coordinator, so microservices prefer Saga plus Outbox with eventual consistency.

sections.s2_technical:
JTA is the Java standard for transactions that span multiple resources. An XA resource is one that supports the XA protocol, which lets an external transaction manager coordinate its commit. A JTA transaction manager like Atomikos or Narayana coordinates these resources. In Spring you would use a `JtaTransactionManager` instead of the usual `DataSourceTransactionManager`. For example, enlisting two XA data sources means a single `@Transactional` method can write to two databases and have them commit together.

Two-phase commit is the protocol underneath. In phase one, the prepare phase, the coordinator asks each resource "can you commit?" Each resource does all the work, writes it to a durable log, locks the rows, and votes yes or no but does not commit yet. In phase two, the commit phase, if every resource voted yes the coordinator tells them all to commit; if any voted no it tells them all to roll back. The guarantee is strong atomicity across all resources.

The problem is the cost. Between phase one and phase two, every resource holds its locks and keeps its transaction open across network round-trips. If the coordinator is slow or a resource is far away, those locks are held for a long time, which kills throughput under load. For a busy bank processing thousands of transfers per second, holding row locks across a network call to another service is unacceptable.

The bigger problem in microservices is coupling and availability. Two-phase commit requires all participants to be available at commit time. If one service is down, the whole transaction cannot complete. This violates the independence that microservices are built for. The coordinator is also a single point of failure: if it crashes after phase one but before phase two, resources are left in an uncertain "in doubt" state, holding locks until the coordinator recovers. Many cloud data stores and message brokers like Kafka do not support XA at all, so you often cannot use two-phase commit even if you wanted to.

The preferred alternative is the Saga pattern. A Saga breaks one big distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each in its own service, each committing independently. If a later step fails, the Saga runs compensating transactions to undo the earlier steps. For example, a transfer across services might be: debit Rajesh's account (local commit), then credit Priya's account (local commit); if the credit fails, run a compensating transaction that credits Rajesh back. There is no global lock and no coordinator holding everything open.

Sagas come in two styles. Orchestration uses a central coordinator service that tells each step what to do next and triggers compensations on failure, which is easier to reason about and monitor. Choreography has each service publish events that the next service listens for, with no central brain, which is more decoupled but harder to trace end to end.

The Outbox pattern solves a subtle problem: you cannot atomically write to your database and publish to Kafka in one transaction because Kafka is not XA. Instead, in the same local database transaction, you write your business row and also insert a row into an outbox table. Because both writes are in the same local transaction, they commit together atomically. A separate relay process then reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, marking them sent. This guarantees that the event is published if and only if the business data committed, giving you at-least-once delivery without any distributed transaction.

All of this accepts eventual consistency. Instead of everything being perfectly consistent at the same instant, the system becomes consistent after a short delay as the steps and events propagate. For a bank, this means the transfer completes in steps and the final state is correct, even if for a brief moment one service has updated and another has not. A senior engineer designs idempotent operations and compensations so retries are safe, because in an eventually consistent system messages can be delivered more than once.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a cross-service money transfer touches two separate services with two separate databases: the Account Service that holds Rajesh's savings account and the Account Service instance that holds Priya's current account, which in a microservice world are independent. We want the money to leave Rajesh and arrive at Priya atomically. The old approach was JTA two-phase commit across both databases, but it held locks across the network and the coordinator became a bottleneck and a single point of failure. This is exactly why we move to a Saga.

Problem 2 — If the debit from Rajesh succeeds but the credit to Priya fails, we must not leave the money in limbo. This is exactly what a compensating transaction does — we credit Rajesh back to undo the debit.

Problem 3 — We also need to publish a "transfer completed" event to Kafka, but we cannot write to our database and publish to Kafka in one atomic step because Kafka is not XA. This is exactly what the Outbox pattern solves — we write the business change and an outbox row in the same local transaction, and a relay publishes it afterward.

What the code will do. The `Account` class holds balance with debit and credit. Two repositories stand in for two services' databases. A `TransferSaga` orchestrates: step one debits Rajesh with a local commit and writes an outbox row, step two credits Priya with a local commit; if step two fails, it runs the compensating transaction to credit Rajesh back. An `OutboxRelay` later publishes the outbox rows. The demo runs a successful Saga and a failing Saga that triggers compensation, showing eventual consistency and no global lock.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a successful transfer of Rs.50,000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001, then a failing transfer of Rs.30,000 from SAV2001 to an invalid account FROZEN9.

Step 1. The successful Saga starts. Step one debits Rajesh Rs.50,000 in its own local transaction and, in the same transaction, writes an outbox row saying "DEBITED SAV2001". This local transaction commits on its own. No global lock is held.

Step 2. Step two credits Priya Rs.50,000 in its own local transaction and writes an outbox row "CREDITED CUR3001". It commits. The Saga is complete. Rajesh is at Rs.950,000 and Priya at Rs.300,000.

Step 3. Later, out of band, the Outbox relay reads the unsent outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, then marks them sent. This is the eventual consistency moment — the event reaches downstream consumers a little after the money moved.

Step 4. The failing Saga starts. Step one debits Rajesh Rs.30,000 and commits locally. Rajesh is temporarily at Rs.920,000.

Step 5. Step two tries to credit FROZEN9, which does not exist, so it throws. The Saga catches this and runs the compensating transaction, crediting Rajesh back Rs.30,000. Rajesh returns to Rs.950,000. The system is consistent again, with no money lost and no global lock ever held.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A distributed transaction spans more than one resource, like two databases or a database and a message broker, and must commit or roll back all of them together. The classic way is JTA coordinating XA resources with two-phase commit. In phase one the coordinator asks every resource to prepare and vote, and in phase two it tells them all to commit if everyone voted yes or roll back if anyone voted no. That gives strict atomicity, but between the two phases every resource holds its locks and keeps its transaction open across network calls.

That cost is why two-phase commit is discouraged in microservices. Holding row locks across a network round-trip destroys throughput under load, every participant must be available at commit time which breaks the independence of services, and the coordinator is a single point of failure. If it crashes between phase one and phase two, resources are left in doubt holding locks until it recovers. On top of that, many modern stores and Kafka do not even support XA, so two-phase commit is often not an option.

In my banking project we moved a cross-service transfer from JTA to a Saga. We broke it into local transactions: debit Rajesh in his service with a local commit, then credit Priya in her service with a local commit. If the credit failed, we ran a compensating transaction that credited Rajesh back, so no money was ever lost and no global lock was ever held. We used an orchestration Saga with a central coordinator because it was easier to monitor and trace than choreography.

We combined this with the Outbox pattern, because we could not atomically write to our database and publish to Kafka. In the same local transaction we wrote the business change and an outbox row, so they committed together, and a separate relay published the outbox rows to Kafka afterward. That gave us reliable at-least-once publishing without any distributed transaction. The tradeoff we accepted was eventual consistency, so we made every operation and compensation idempotent so retries were safe. The way I summarize it in an interview is that two-phase commit buys strict atomicity at the price of availability and scale, and in microservices we almost always prefer Saga plus Outbox with eventual consistency and idempotency instead.

answers.question: Why do bulk @Query UPDATE and DELETE statements need @Modifying and @Transactional? What do clearAutomatically and flushAutomatically do, and how do they prevent a stale persistence context?
answers.shortTitle: @Modifying + @Transactional on @Query UPDATE/DELETE

s1_definition.profdef: In Spring Data JPA, a custom `@Query` that performs an UPDATE or DELETE must be annotated with `@Modifying` so Spring knows to call `executeUpdate` instead of expecting a result set, and it must run inside a transaction, so you add `@Transactional`. A bulk modifying query runs directly against the database and bypasses the persistence context, so entities already loaded into the first-level cache can become stale. The `flushAutomatically` attribute flushes pending changes to the database before the query runs, and the `clearAutomatically` attribute clears the persistence context after the query runs so that subsequent reads fetch fresh data from the database.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India has photocopies of several account pages on his desk (the persistence context). Now the manager issues a bulk order: "add one percent interest to every savings account" straight into the master ledger (a bulk UPDATE). The clerk's photocopies are now out of date because they still show the old balances. `flushAutomatically` makes the clerk first write any pending edits into the master ledger before the bulk order runs, and `clearAutomatically` makes the clerk throw away his stale photocopies after the bulk order so that next time he needs an account he fetches a fresh page from the master ledger.
s1_definition.oneliner: Bulk UPDATE/DELETE queries skip the persistence context, so use `@Modifying` with `@Transactional` and set `clearAutomatically = true` to avoid reading stale cached entities afterward.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Spring Data JPA, a custom `@Query` that performs an UPDATE or DELETE must be annotated with `@Modifying` so Spring knows to call `executeUpdate` instead of expecting a result set, and it must run inside a transaction, so you add `@Transactional`. A bulk modifying query runs directly against the database and bypasses the persistence context, so entities already loaded into the first-level cache can become stale. The `flushAutomatically` attribute flushes pending changes to the database before the query runs, and the `clearAutomatically` attribute clears the persistence context after the query runs so that subsequent reads fetch fresh data from the database.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India has photocopies of several account pages on his desk (the persistence context). Now the manager issues a bulk order: "add one percent interest to every savings account" straight into the master ledger (a bulk UPDATE). The clerk's photocopies are now out of date because they still show the old balances. `flushAutomatically` makes the clerk first write any pending edits into the master ledger before the bulk order runs, and `clearAutomatically` makes the clerk throw away his stale photocopies after the bulk order so that next time he needs an account he fetches a fresh page from the master ledger.

**One line to remember:** Bulk UPDATE/DELETE queries skip the persistence context, so use `@Modifying` with `@Transactional` and set `clearAutomatically = true` to avoid reading stale cached entities afterward.

sections.s2_technical:
A normal derived query or a `@Query` with a SELECT returns data. But when your JPQL is an UPDATE or DELETE, Spring Data cannot treat it the same way. You must add `@Modifying` so Spring calls `Query.executeUpdate()`, which returns the number of affected rows instead of a list. For example `@Modifying @Query("UPDATE Account a SET a.balance = a.balance + :interest WHERE a.type = 'SAVINGS'") int applyInterest(@Param("interest") BigDecimal interest);` returns how many accounts were updated.

A modifying query changes data, so it must run in a transaction. If there is no active transaction you get a `TransactionRequiredException`. You can put `@Transactional` on the repository method, but the cleaner and more common practice is to put it on the service method that calls the repository, so the whole business operation is one transaction. For example the service method `applyMonthlyInterest` is annotated `@Transactional` and calls the modifying repository method inside it.

The crucial point is that a bulk modifying query runs directly as SQL against the database and completely bypasses the persistence context, also called the first-level cache. Hibernate does not know which in-memory entities the bulk statement affected. So if you already loaded Rajesh's account into the persistence context and then run a bulk UPDATE that changes his balance in the database, the in-memory copy still shows the old balance. Reading it again in the same transaction returns the stale cached value, not the new database value. This is the stale persistence context problem.

The `clearAutomatically` attribute solves this. When set to true, Spring clears the persistence context after the modifying query runs, so Hibernate forgets all the entities it had cached. The next time you load any entity, Hibernate goes back to the database and gets fresh data. For example `@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true) @Query("UPDATE Account a SET a.status = 'FROZEN' WHERE a.balance < 0") int freezeOverdrawn();` ensures that after the freeze, any account you read reflects the new status. The default is false, which is why people get confused when their reads after a bulk update show old values.

The `flushAutomatically` attribute handles the other direction. When set to true, Spring flushes any pending changes in the persistence context to the database before the modifying query runs. This matters when you have made in-memory changes that have not been written yet, and your bulk query depends on them. For example if you changed some accounts' types in memory and then run a bulk UPDATE that filters by type, you want those pending changes flushed first so the bulk query sees them. The default is false, so by default Hibernate does not force a flush before the bulk statement, which can cause the bulk query to run against data that does not yet reflect your pending changes.

A senior-level nuance is that the right combination for most bulk operations is `@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true, flushAutomatically = true)` plus `@Transactional`. Flush first so the database reflects pending work, run the bulk statement, then clear so later reads are fresh. Another nuance is that bulk UPDATE and DELETE statements do not cascade and do not trigger entity lifecycle callbacks or optimistic locking version increments, because they bypass the entity layer entirely. So if you have `@Version` optimistic locking or `@PreUpdate` callbacks, a bulk statement will not honor them, which is a deliberate tradeoff you accept for performance on large updates. For small numbers of entities you would load and modify them normally so lifecycle and versioning work; for millions of rows you use a bulk modifying query for speed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, interest must be applied to every savings account at month end. There could be millions of accounts. Loading each one into memory, adding interest, and saving it back would be painfully slow and use huge memory. This is exactly why we use a bulk `@Query` UPDATE with `@Modifying` — one SQL statement updates all savings accounts at once.

Problem 2 — A developer loaded Rajesh's account earlier in the same transaction, then ran the bulk interest update, then read Rajesh's balance again and saw the old value without the interest. This is exactly the stale persistence context problem, and `clearAutomatically = true` fixes it by clearing the cache so the re-read fetches the new balance from the database.

Problem 3 — Before applying interest, some accounts had their type changed to SAVINGS in memory but not yet flushed. The bulk update filters by type SAVINGS, so it would miss those accounts. This is exactly what `flushAutomatically = true` fixes by flushing pending changes to the database before the bulk update runs.

What the code will do. The `Account` entity has id, holderName, type, and balance. The `AccountRepository` has a bulk `applyInterest` modifying query with both flush and clear set to true. The `InterestService` is transactional, demonstrates loading Rajesh before the bulk update, runs the update, and reads Rajesh again to prove the value is now fresh. The demo shows the stale read problem avoided and the correct final balances.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 1 percent monthly interest rate. Rajesh (SAV2001) is a savings account with Rs.1,000,000. Priya (CUR3001) is a current account with Rs.250,000, which should not get interest.

Step 1. The transactional service method starts. It loads Rajesh's account by id. Hibernate puts a copy into the persistence context showing the balance of Rs.1,000,000. The log confirms the cached before-value.

Step 2. The service calls the repository's modifying query. Because flushAutomatically is true, Hibernate first flushes any pending changes to the database so the bulk statement sees the latest committed state.

Step 3. The bulk UPDATE runs directly as SQL. It adds 1 percent to every savings account's balance in the database. Rajesh's database row is now Rs.1,010,000. Priya is a current account, so her row is untouched at Rs.250,000. This statement bypasses the persistence context entirely, so the in-memory copy of Rajesh still says Rs.1,000,000.

Step 4. Because clearAutomatically is true, Hibernate clears the persistence context after the bulk update. The stale copy of Rajesh is discarded.

Step 5. The service reads Rajesh again. Since the cache was cleared, Hibernate fetches a fresh row from the database and returns Rs.1,010,000, the correct new value. Without clearAutomatically, this read would have returned the stale Rs.1,000,000.

```
2026-10-23 16:20:01 [FINE   ] FLUSH: pending changes written to DB
2026-10-23 16:20:01 [INFO   ] Bulk UPDATE applied interest to 1 savings accounts
2026-10-23 16:20:01 [FINE   ] CLEAR: persistence context emptied, next read hits DB
2026-10-23 16:20:01 [FINE   ] Loading SAV2001 from DB into persistence context
2026-10-23 16:20:01 [INFO   ] Rajesh balance AFTER bulk update (fresh) = 1010000.00
2026-10-23 16:20:01 [INFO   ] Priya (CURRENT, not a savings account) = 250000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I write a custom query in Spring Data JPA that performs an UPDATE or DELETE instead of a SELECT, I must add the Modifying annotation so Spring calls executeUpdate and returns the affected row count rather than expecting a result set. Because it changes data, it must run inside a transaction, so I put the Transactional annotation on the service method that drives the operation, otherwise I get a TransactionRequiredException.

The subtle part that interviewers probe is cache coherence. A bulk modifying query runs directly as SQL against the database and completely bypasses the persistence context, the first-level cache. So if I already loaded an entity into memory and then run a bulk update that changes it in the database, the in-memory copy is now stale, and reading it again in the same transaction returns the old value. In my banking project this bit us during the month-end interest batch. We loaded Rajesh's savings account, ran a bulk update that added one percent interest to every savings account, then read his balance again and saw the old amount because the cached copy was never updated.

The fix is the two attributes on the Modifying annotation. clearAutomatically set to true clears the persistence context after the bulk query runs, so the next read of any entity fetches fresh data from the database instead of a stale cached copy. flushAutomatically set to true flushes any pending in-memory changes to the database before the bulk query runs, so the bulk statement operates on the latest state. For almost every bulk operation I use both together along with the Transactional annotation: flush first, run the bulk statement, then clear.

The last thing I always mention is the tradeoff. Because bulk statements bypass the entity layer, they do not cascade to related entities, they do not trigger lifecycle callbacks like PreUpdate, and they do not increment optimistic locking versions. That is the deliberate price for being able to update millions of rows in one fast SQL statement. For a handful of entities I would load and modify them normally so versioning and callbacks work, but for a huge batch like applying interest to every savings account, the bulk modifying query with clear and flush enabled is the right tool.

answers.question: Should @Transactional go on the class, the implementation, or the interface? Explain how JDK dynamic proxies differ from CGLIB proxies and why you should always put @Transactional on the implementation.
answers.shortTitle: @Transactional on class vs interface — JDK proxy vs CGLIB

s1_definition.profdef: Spring applies `@Transactional` through an AOP proxy that wraps your bean and begins, commits, or rolls back the transaction around the method call. Spring can create two kinds of proxies: a JDK dynamic proxy, which implements the bean's interfaces and only sees annotations on interface methods, or a CGLIB proxy, which subclasses the concrete class and sees annotations on the class. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB proxying since Spring 5.x. Because a CGLIB proxy subclasses the implementation and cannot reliably read interface-level annotations, you should always put `@Transactional` on the implementation class or its methods, not on the interface, so it works regardless of which proxy type is used.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the proxy as a security guard standing in front of the real banking clerk. With a JDK proxy, the guard only reads the rulebook posted on the public counter (the interface) — if the "transaction required" rule is written there, he enforces it. With a CGLIB proxy, the guard is actually a stand-in wearing the clerk's uniform (a subclass), and he only reads the rules written in the clerk's own personal notebook (the implementation), not the public counter. Since Spring Boot hires the uniform-wearing stand-in by default, you must write the transaction rule in the clerk's own notebook — the implementation — or it gets ignored.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default, which proxies the concrete class, so always annotate the implementation, not the interface, or `@Transactional` may be silently ignored.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spring applies `@Transactional` through an AOP proxy that wraps your bean and begins, commits, or rolls back the transaction around the method call. Spring can create two kinds of proxies: a JDK dynamic proxy, which implements the bean's interfaces and only sees annotations on interface methods, or a CGLIB proxy, which subclasses the concrete class and sees annotations on the class. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB proxying since Spring 5.x. Because a CGLIB proxy subclasses the implementation and cannot reliably read interface-level annotations, you should always put `@Transactional` on the implementation class or its methods, not on the interface, so it works regardless of which proxy type is used.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the proxy as a security guard standing in front of the real banking clerk. With a JDK proxy, the guard only reads the rulebook posted on the public counter (the interface) — if the "transaction required" rule is written there, he enforces it. With a CGLIB proxy, the guard is actually a stand-in wearing the clerk's uniform (a subclass), and he only reads the rules written in the clerk's own personal notebook (the implementation), not the public counter. Since Spring Boot hires the uniform-wearing stand-in by default, you must write the transaction rule in the clerk's own notebook — the implementation — or it gets ignored.

**One line to remember:** Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default, which proxies the concrete class, so always annotate the implementation, not the interface, or `@Transactional` may be silently ignored.

sections.s2_technical:
Spring does not add transaction behavior to your bytecode directly. Instead it creates a proxy object that wraps your bean. When someone calls a method on the proxy, the proxy starts a transaction, calls the real method, and then commits or rolls back. This is why `@Transactional` only works on calls that come through the proxy from outside the bean.

There are two proxy mechanisms. A JDK dynamic proxy is created by the JDK's `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`. It works only if your bean implements at least one interface, because the proxy itself implements those same interfaces. A JDK proxy reads the transaction metadata from the interface methods it implements. A CGLIB proxy is created by generating a subclass of your concrete class at runtime and overriding its methods. It does not need an interface because it extends the class directly, and it reads the metadata from the concrete class.

Historically, Spring used JDK proxies when the bean had an interface and fell back to CGLIB only when there was no interface. But since Spring 5 and Spring Boot 2, the default changed: `@EnableTransactionManagement` and Spring Boot both default to `proxyTargetClass = true`, which means CGLIB is used even when interfaces are present. So in a modern Spring Boot app, your service is almost always wrapped by a CGLIB subclass proxy.

This is exactly why the placement of the annotation matters. A CGLIB proxy subclasses the implementation, so it reliably sees `@Transactional` on the implementation class and its methods. It does not reliably pick up annotations that exist only on the interface, because CGLIB is working at the class level, not the interface level. If you put `@Transactional` only on the interface and Spring uses CGLIB, the annotation can be silently ignored and your method runs with no transaction at all. That is a dangerous bug in a bank, because a transfer that should have been atomic might partially apply.

The safe and recommended practice is to always put `@Transactional` on the implementation. For example, define a plain interface `TransferService` with no transaction annotations, and put `@Transactional` on the implementation class `TransferServiceImpl` or on its methods. For example `public class TransferServiceImpl implements TransferService { @Transactional public void transfer(...) { ... } }`. This works under both JDK and CGLIB proxies, so it is robust no matter how Spring is configured.

There are a few more practical consequences of CGLIB. Because CGLIB creates a subclass, your class and the transactional methods cannot be `final`, and the class cannot be `final` either, since you cannot subclass or override final things. A `final` method simply will not be proxied, so its `@Transactional` is ignored. Also, CGLIB cannot proxy private methods, so `@Transactional` on a private method does nothing. And the self-invocation rule still applies: if a method inside the bean calls another method on `this`, the call does not go through the proxy, so the second method's `@Transactional` is ignored regardless of proxy type.

A senior-level summary is that the Spring Framework reference documentation itself recommends annotating concrete classes rather than interfaces, precisely because the choice of proxy strategy affects whether interface annotations are honored. Putting the annotation on the implementation removes all ambiguity. If you genuinely need interface-based JDK proxies, you can set `proxyTargetClass = false`, but even then annotating the implementation is the defensive choice.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a developer defined a `TransferService` interface and put `@Transactional` on the interface method, then wrote a `TransferServiceImpl` without the annotation. In testing, transfers that should have rolled back on failure instead left money half-moved. This is exactly the JDK-proxy-versus-CGLIB problem — because Spring Boot used CGLIB by default, the interface annotation was ignored and the method ran with no transaction.

Problem 2 — Another developer made a service method `final` for safety, and its `@Transactional` silently stopped working because CGLIB cannot override a final method. This is exactly why transactional classes and methods must not be final.

Problem 3 — The fix for both was moving the annotation to the implementation. This is exactly the recommended practice: annotate the concrete class so it works under any proxy type.

What the code will do. The `Account` class holds balance with debit and credit. A `TransferService` interface declares the transfer method with no annotations. A `TransferServiceImpl` puts `@Transactional` on its transfer method so both JDK and CGLIB proxies honor it. The demo simulates a CGLIB proxy wrapping the implementation, shows a successful transfer committing and a failing transfer rolling back, and contrasts what would happen if the annotation were only on the interface.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a successful transfer of Rs.50,000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001, then a failing transfer of Rs.9,999,999 that must roll back.

Step 1. The caller invokes transfer on the proxy, not on the real implementation. Because Spring Boot uses CGLIB, the proxy is a subclass of the implementation. It inspects the concrete class method and finds the Transactional annotation there. Since the annotation is on the implementation, it is honored.

Step 2. The proxy begins a transaction, then calls the real transfer method on the target. Rajesh has enough balance, so he is debited Rs.50,000 and Priya credited Rs.50,000.

Step 3. The real method returns normally. The proxy commits. Rajesh is now Rs.950,000 and Priya Rs.300,000.

Step 4. The caller invokes transfer again for Rs.9,999,999. The proxy begins a new transaction and calls the real method.

Step 5. Rajesh does not have Rs.9,999,999, so the real method throws. The proxy catches the exception, rolls back, and re-throws. Because of the rollback, nothing changed: Rajesh stays at Rs.950,000 and Priya at Rs.300,000. Had the annotation been only on the interface, CGLIB would not have seen it, no transaction would have started, and a partial debit could have leaked.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring does not weave transaction code into your bytecode directly. It wraps your bean in an AOP proxy that begins the transaction, calls your real method, and then commits or rolls back. There are two kinds of proxy. A JDK dynamic proxy implements your bean's interfaces and reads the Transactional annotation from the interface methods. A CGLIB proxy generates a subclass of your concrete class at runtime and reads the annotation from the class itself. Since Spring 5 and Spring Boot 2, the default is CGLIB, with proxyTargetClass set to true, even when your bean has an interface.

This default is exactly why annotation placement matters. A CGLIB proxy subclasses the implementation, so it reliably sees Transactional on the implementation class and its methods, but it does not reliably pick up an annotation that lives only on the interface. In my banking project a developer once put Transactional on the interface method and left the implementation bare. Because Spring Boot used CGLIB, the annotation was silently ignored, no transaction was ever started, and a failing transfer left money half-moved instead of rolling back. That is a serious bug in a bank.

The fix, and the practice I always follow, is to keep the interface clean and put Transactional on the implementation class or its methods. That works under both JDK and CGLIB proxies, so it is robust no matter how Spring is configured. The Spring reference documentation itself recommends annotating concrete classes rather than interfaces for exactly this reason.

There are a few related CGLIB rules I always keep in mind. Because CGLIB creates a subclass, the transactional class and its methods must not be final, since a final method cannot be overridden and its annotation will be ignored. CGLIB also cannot proxy private methods, so Transactional on a private method does nothing. And the self-invocation rule still applies under any proxy: if a method calls another annotated method on this, the call does not go through the proxy and the annotation is skipped. So my rule of thumb is simple: always annotate the implementation, keep transactional classes and methods non-final and public, and never rely on self-invocation for transactions.

answers.shortTitle: How @Transactional works — AOP proxy, begin/commit/rollback, key attributes

s1_definition.profdef: `@Transactional` is implemented via an AOP proxy (CGLIB subclass). When a method annotated with `@Transactional` is called from OUTSIDE the class, the proxy intercepts, gets a DB connection from HikariCP, sets `auto-commit=false`, calls the real method, and either commits on success or rolls back on `RuntimeException`. Key attributes: `propagation` (REQUIRED default — join existing or create new), `isolation` (database-level read consistency), `readOnly` (skip dirty checking, hint for read replica), `timeout` (fail if TX exceeds N seconds), `rollbackFor` (which exceptions trigger rollback — only `RuntimeException` by default).
s1_definition.analogy: @Transactional is the bank's "all-or-nothing" rule: debit Rs.50,000 from Rajesh AND credit Rs.50,000 to Priya — both succeed or neither happens. The proxy is the vault door that opens (begin), lets you work (method), and either seals the changes (commit) or undoes everything (rollback).

sections.s2_technical:
The proxy flow: `TransactionInterceptor` calls `TransactionAspectSupport.invokeWithinTransaction()` which uses the `PlatformTransactionManager` to begin a TX. The connection is bound to the current thread via `TransactionSynchronizationManager` (ThreadLocal). All repository calls on that thread share the SAME connection. On success, the proxy calls `commit()`. On `RuntimeException`/`Error`, it calls `rollback()`. On checked exceptions, it COMMITS by default (fix with `rollbackFor=Exception.class`).

Key attributes: `@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRED, isolation = READ_COMMITTED, readOnly = false, timeout = 30, rollbackFor = Exception.class)`.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Transactional annotation works through an AOP proxy that Spring creates around the bean. When a transactional method is called from outside the class, the proxy intercepts the call, obtains a database connection from the HikariCP pool, disables auto-commit to begin a transaction, and binds the connection to the current thread via TransactionSynchronizationManager. All repository calls within that method share the same connection through ThreadLocal lookup, ensuring they participate in the same transaction. On successful completion, the proxy commits. On RuntimeException or Error, the proxy rolls back. Critically, checked exceptions do NOT trigger rollback by default — you must add rollbackFor equals Exception.class.

In my NEFT transfer service, the transfer method debits the sender and credits the receiver within a single transaction. If the credit fails because the receiver's account is frozen, the proxy catches the RuntimeException and rolls back the entire transaction, including the debit. The sender's balance remains unchanged — atomicity is preserved. The method must be public (CGLIB cannot override private), must be called from outside the class (self-invocation bypasses the proxy), and uses pessimistic locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE to prevent concurrent modification of the same account.

The key attributes are: isolation controls what concurrent transactions can see (READ_COMMITTED is the PostgreSQL default), propagation controls how nested transactional calls behave (REQUIRED joins the existing transaction or creates a new one), readOnly skips Hibernate dirty checking and hints the driver to route to a read replica, timeout fails the transaction after N seconds to prevent connection pool starvation, and rollbackFor specifies which exception types trigger rollback beyond the default RuntimeException.
