s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `TransactionSynchronization` is a Spring callback interface that lets you hook custom logic into the lifecycle of the current transaction. You register an implementation with `TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(...)` while a transaction is active, and Spring then calls your callbacks at well-defined points: `beforeCommit` just before the commit is issued, `afterCommit` only after a successful commit, `beforeCompletion` just before the transaction ends either way, and `afterCompletion` after the transaction has finished with a status telling you whether it committed or rolled back. These callbacks are the correct place to put side effects that must be aligned with the real database outcome.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh walks into the National Bank of India to transfer Rs.50,000 to Priya. The teller does not send Rajesh an SMS the moment he fills the form, because the form might still be rejected. The teller waits until the vault actually records the money movement and the register is stamped, and only then sends the SMS confirmation. If the form is rejected, the teller sends a failure message instead. `TransactionSynchronization` is exactly this well-mannered teller. It says, "I will send the SMS only after the money truly moved, never before, and I will clear my scratch notes whether the transfer passed or failed."

**One line to remember:** TransactionSynchronization lets you run the right side effect at the right moment in the transaction's life — notify only after commit, clean up always after completion.

sections.s2_technical:
Spring keeps a per-thread list of synchronizations bound to the active transaction. You add to that list by calling `TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(...)`. This only works when a real transaction is in progress, which you can check with `TransactionSynchronizationManager.isSynchronizationActive()`. If you register outside an active transaction, Spring throws an `IllegalStateException`, so always guard the registration.

The `beforeCommit` method runs just before Spring tells the database to commit. It receives a boolean `readOnly` flag. This is the last moment where you can still influence the transaction, for example flushing a final piece of state or doing a last validation. For example, you could verify an invariant before the money is locked in: `public void beforeCommit(boolean readOnly) { if (!ledgerBalanced) throw new IllegalStateException("Ledger not balanced, aborting commit"); }`. If you throw here, the commit is turned into a rollback, which is powerful but must be used carefully.

The `beforeCompletion` method runs just before the transaction is finalized, whether it will commit or roll back. It is commonly used to release resources that must be released regardless of outcome, such as returning a borrowed object to a pool. For example: `public void beforeCompletion() { resourceLock.release(); }`.

The `afterCommit` method is the one banking systems care about most. It runs only if the transaction committed successfully. This is where you send the SMS to Rajesh, publish a Kafka event, or call an external payment confirmation, because at this point the money movement is durable and real. For example: `public void afterCommit() { notificationService.sendSms(rajesh, "Rs.50000 transferred to CUR3001"); }`. If you sent that SMS inside the transaction and the commit later failed, Rajesh would get a lie.

The `afterCompletion` method always runs at the very end, and it receives a status integer: `STATUS_COMMITTED`, `STATUS_ROLLED_BACK`, or `STATUS_UNKNOWN`. This is the place to clear thread-local caches, evict stale cache entries, and do cleanup that must happen no matter what. For example: `public void afterCompletion(int status) { cache.evict(accountId); if (status == STATUS_ROLLED_BACK) metrics.incrementFailed(); }`. A senior-level nuance is that an exception thrown in `afterCommit` or `afterCompletion` does not roll back the transaction, because by then the commit decision is already made; it is only logged, so you must handle your own failures there.

A common modern alternative is `@TransactionalEventListener` with its `phase` attribute of `AFTER_COMMIT`, which is a higher-level wrapper around exactly this mechanism. But understanding the raw `TransactionSynchronization` interface shows the interviewer you know what happens underneath.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, customers complained that they received an SMS saying "Rs.50,000 transferred successfully" even though the money never actually left their account. The reason was that the old code sent the SMS in the middle of the transfer method, before the database commit. When the commit later failed because of a constraint violation, the money stayed put but the SMS had already gone out. Rajesh trusted the SMS, assumed the rent was paid, and a dispute followed. This is exactly what the `afterCommit` callback fixes — the SMS is sent only after the database truly commits, so the message can never lie.

Problem 2 — The bank cached account balances in memory for fast display. After a transfer, the cached balance for Rajesh and Priya became stale and showed the old numbers. The cache had to be cleared whether the transfer succeeded or failed, because even a rolled-back attempt could have touched in-flight state. This is exactly what the `afterCompletion` callback does — it runs at the end no matter what, so it is the perfect place to evict the cache.

Problem 3 — The compliance team needed a final balance check right before the commit, to make sure the total money in the system never changed during a transfer, only moved between accounts. This last-second invariant check is exactly what `beforeCommit` is for — it runs just before the commit and can abort it if something is wrong.

What the code will do. We model an `Account` with debit and credit. A `TransferService` performs the transfer inside a simulated transaction and registers a `TransferSynchronization` with the transaction manager. The synchronization implements `beforeCommit` to verify the ledger total, `afterCommit` to send the success SMS through a `NotificationService`, and `afterCompletion` to clear balances from a `BalanceCache`. A small transaction runner simulates Spring beginning, committing, and rolling back a transaction and firing the callbacks in the correct order. The demo shows one successful transfer that sends an SMS and one failing transfer that does not send an SMS but still clears the cache.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a successful transfer of Rs.50,000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001, then a failing transfer of Rs.9,999,999.

Step 1. The caller invokes transfer. Before any work, the service reads the total money in the bank, which is Rs.1,250,000, and remembers it as the expected total. It then registers a synchronization object with the transaction.

Step 2. The transaction begins. The body runs: Rajesh has enough, so he is debited Rs.50,000 and Priya is credited Rs.50,000. The cache is updated with the new balances.

Step 3. Just before commit, `beforeCommit` runs. It re-reads the total money, which is still Rs.1,250,000. The money only moved, it did not change, so the invariant holds and the commit is allowed.

Step 4. `beforeCompletion` runs to release transfer resources. The transaction commits. Because the commit succeeded, `afterCommit` runs and the SMS "Rs.50000 transferred to CUR3001 successfully" is sent to Rajesh. This is the first moment the SMS could truthfully be sent.

Step 5. `afterCompletion` runs with status committed. It clears the cache entries for both accounts and logs a clean commit.

Step 6. The second transfer begins. The body throws because Rajesh does not have Rs.9,999,999. The commit never happens. `beforeCommit` and `afterCommit` are skipped entirely, so no false SMS is sent. `beforeCompletion` runs, the transaction rolls back, and `afterCompletion` runs with status rolled back, which clears the cache and logs the failure. Balances stay at Rs.950,000 and Rs.300,000.

sections.s6_takeaway:
TransactionSynchronization is Spring's callback interface for hooking custom logic into the lifecycle of the current transaction. I register an implementation using TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization while a transaction is active, and Spring then calls my callbacks at precise moments. The beforeCommit method runs just before the commit and is my last chance to enforce an invariant or abort. The beforeCompletion method runs just before the transaction ends, pass or fail, and is good for releasing resources. The afterCommit method runs only if the transaction actually committed. And the afterCompletion method always runs at the end with a status telling me whether it committed or rolled back.

The single most important rule I follow is that any side effect which the outside world will trust must go in afterCommit, never inside the transaction body. In my banking project at the National Bank of India, we once sent the transfer SMS in the middle of the transfer method. When a later commit failed, the money stayed put but the customer had already been told it succeeded, which caused real disputes. Moving the SMS into afterCommit fixed it completely, because afterCommit only fires when the money movement is truly durable. A failed transfer now sends no SMS at all, so the message can never lie.

I use afterCompletion for cleanup that must happen no matter the outcome, such as evicting stale account balances from our cache. Because afterCompletion runs on both commit and rollback, the cache is always cleared, and I can branch on the status to increment a failure metric when it rolled back. I also keep beforeCommit for a final ledger check that confirms the total money in the system did not change, only moved between accounts.

A couple of senior nuances I always mention. Registration only works inside an active transaction, so I guard it with isSynchronizationActive to avoid an IllegalStateException. And an exception thrown inside afterCommit or afterCompletion does not roll back the transaction, because the commit decision is already final by then, so I handle my own errors there rather than relying on the transaction to protect me. In modern code I often use the higher-level @TransactionalEventListener with phase AFTER_COMMIT, which is built on this exact mechanism, but understanding the raw synchronization callbacks is what lets me reason correctly about when every side effect runs.

answers.question: Why can @Transactional(readOnly=true) cause an INSERT or UPDATE to silently disappear with no error? Explain how FlushMode.MANUAL means Hibernate never flushes pending changes, how a class-level readOnly setting is inherited by a write method, and how to fix it so writes are never silently dropped.
answers.shortTitle: @Transactional(readOnly=true) silently DROPS writes — the inherited-readOnly trap

s1_definition.profdef: When you mark a method with `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`, Spring tells the underlying Hibernate session to switch its flush mode to `FlushMode.MANUAL`. In this mode, Hibernate stops automatically flushing the persistence context, which means any `INSERT` or `UPDATE` you queue by changing a managed entity or calling `save()` is held in memory and never written to the database. There is no exception and no warning; the pending SQL is simply discarded when the transaction ends. The trap becomes severe when `readOnly = true` is placed at the class level, because every method, including methods that perform writes, inherits that read-only setting unless it is explicitly overridden.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India gives a teller a special "inquiry only" stamp for the whole day. With that stamp, the teller can look up Rajesh's balance and read Priya's statement, but the vault ignores any instruction to actually move money, and it does so silently without complaining. Now imagine a new transfer counter is opened under the same "inquiry only" supervisor. The teller at that counter fills out the transfer form for Rajesh, tells the customer it is done, but because the whole department is stamped "inquiry only," the vault quietly throws the form in the bin. Rajesh walks away thinking Rs.50,000 moved, but nothing happened. That silent discarding is exactly what inherited readOnly does to a write method.
s1_definition.oneliner: readOnly=true flips Hibernate to manual flush, so writes under it vanish without error — never let a write method inherit a class-level readOnly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When you mark a method with `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`, Spring tells the underlying Hibernate session to switch its flush mode to `FlushMode.MANUAL`. In this mode, Hibernate stops automatically flushing the persistence context, which means any `INSERT` or `UPDATE` you queue by changing a managed entity or calling `save()` is held in memory and never written to the database. There is no exception and no warning; the pending SQL is simply discarded when the transaction ends. The trap becomes severe when `readOnly = true` is placed at the class level, because every method, including methods that perform writes, inherits that read-only setting unless it is explicitly overridden.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India gives a teller a special "inquiry only" stamp for the whole day. With that stamp, the teller can look up Rajesh's balance and read Priya's statement, but the vault ignores any instruction to actually move money, and it does so silently without complaining. Now imagine a new transfer counter is opened under the same "inquiry only" supervisor. The teller at that counter fills out the transfer form for Rajesh, tells the customer it is done, but because the whole department is stamped "inquiry only," the vault quietly throws the form in the bin. Rajesh walks away thinking Rs.50,000 moved, but nothing happened. That silent discarding is exactly what inherited readOnly does to a write method.

**One line to remember:** readOnly=true flips Hibernate to manual flush, so writes under it vanish without error — never let a write method inherit a class-level readOnly.

sections.s2_technical:
The `readOnly` flag on `@Transactional` is a hint that travels down several layers. At the JDBC level Spring may call `Connection.setReadOnly(true)`, which some databases use for routing to read replicas. But the behavior that bites developers is at the Hibernate level: Spring sets the session's flush mode to `FlushMode.MANUAL`. For example, `@Transactional(readOnly = true) public Account getAccount(String id) { return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); }` is correct because it only reads.

Normally Hibernate uses `FlushMode.AUTO`, which means it automatically flushes pending changes to the database before a query runs and before the transaction commits. Flushing is the act of translating the in-memory changes in the persistence context into actual `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` statements. With `FlushMode.MANUAL`, that automatic flush is turned off entirely. Hibernate will only flush if you call `session.flush()` by hand, which you almost never do in normal Spring code.

So here is the exact failure. Suppose you write `@Transactional(readOnly = true) public void renameHolder(String id, String newName) { Account a = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); a.setHolderName(newName); }`. You changed a managed entity, which normally produces an `UPDATE` at commit. But because the flush mode is manual, Hibernate never flushes, the `UPDATE` is never generated, and the transaction commits as read-only. The name change is lost, and crucially no exception is thrown. The same happens with an explicit `repo.save(newEntity)` under readOnly: the `INSERT` is queued in the persistence context and then discarded.

The most dangerous variant is class-level inheritance. If you write `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` on the whole service class because most methods are queries, every method inherits it. A method like `createAccount(...)` or `transfer(...)` that performs writes will silently become a no-op for its database changes. The code compiles, the tests that check return values may pass, and the bug only surfaces when someone notices the data never changed. For example, a class annotated `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` with a `public void transfer(...)` method will debit and credit entities in memory, log success, and commit nothing.

The fix is disciplined and simple. Use `readOnly = true` only on genuine query methods, never at the class level of a service that also writes. If you must have a class-level default, override every write method with `@Transactional(readOnly = false)` or just `@Transactional`, because the method-level annotation wins over the class-level one. For example: `@Transactional public void transfer(...) { ... }` placed on the write method restores `FlushMode.AUTO` and the writes flush normally. A senior-level habit is to prefer method-level annotations and to treat readOnly as something you add deliberately to a read method, not something you sprinkle on a class.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a developer created an `AccountService` class. Most of its methods were lookups, so to optimize performance the developer put `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` on the entire class. This felt clever because read-only transactions let Hibernate skip dirty checking and let the database route to read replicas. This is exactly the setup that creates the trap: the class-level readOnly becomes the default for every method, including ones that write.

Problem 2 — The same class had a `createAccount` method and a `transfer` method that performed writes. Because they inherited the class-level readOnly, Hibernate ran them under FlushMode.MANUAL. The new account was built in memory, the transfer debited and credited entities in memory, and the methods returned success, but nothing was ever flushed to the database. This is exactly the silent write-drop problem — INSERT and UPDATE statements queued in the persistence context were discarded at commit with no error.

Problem 3 — The operations team only discovered the bug when a customer called asking why his new account did not exist and why a transfer he was told succeeded had never happened. The fix was to remove the blanket class-level readOnly, keep readOnly only on the true query methods, and put an explicit writable @Transactional on every write method so the method-level setting overrides any default. This is exactly how you make writes reliable again.

What the code will do. We model an `Account` with debit and credit. An `AccountRepository` simulates a Hibernate persistence context that flushes to a backing store only when flush mode is AUTO, and silently discards pending changes when flush mode is MANUAL. A `BrokenAccountService` demonstrates the bug by running a write under readOnly and losing it. A `FixedAccountService` shows the correct design where query methods are readOnly and write methods are explicitly writable. The demo runs the broken transfer, shows the money did not move, then runs the fixed transfer and shows it worked.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of Rs.50,000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001, run first through the broken service and then through the fixed service.

Step 1. The broken service runs. Because it inherits a class-level readOnly, Spring sets the Hibernate flush mode to MANUAL. This is the hidden switch that will cause the write to disappear.

Step 2. The broken service loads managed copies of Rajesh and Priya, debits Rs.50,000 from Rajesh, credits Rs.50,000 to Priya, and logs success. At this point the changes exist only in the in-memory persistence context, not the database.

Step 3. The transaction commits. Because the flush mode is MANUAL, Hibernate does not flush, so the queued UPDATE statements are discarded. No exception is thrown. The database still shows Rajesh at Rs.1,000,000 and Priya at Rs.250,000. The money never moved, even though the code said it did.

Step 4. The fixed service runs its transfer. Because the write method carries a writable @Transactional, the flush mode is AUTO. It loads managed copies, checks the balance, debits and credits, and logs success.

Step 5. The transaction commits. With AUTO flush, Hibernate translates the dirty entities into UPDATE statements and writes them to the database. Now Rajesh is Rs.950,000 and Priya is Rs.300,000. The write survived because the flush mode was correct.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The reason @Transactional(readOnly = true) can make a write silently disappear is that Spring uses it as a hint and switches the Hibernate session's flush mode to manual. Normally Hibernate runs in automatic flush mode, so before a query and at commit it automatically turns the in-memory changes in the persistence context into INSERT and UPDATE statements. Under readOnly it sets flush mode to manual, which means that automatic flush never happens. Any entity you modified or saved stays in memory and is quietly discarded when the transaction commits. There is no exception and no warning, which is exactly what makes this bug so dangerous.

The trap becomes severe when readOnly is placed at the class level. In my banking project at the National Bank of India, a developer put readOnly true on the whole AccountService class because most methods were lookups and read-only transactions are a genuine performance optimization. The problem was that the createAccount and transfer methods in the same class inherited that read-only setting. They debited and credited entities in memory, returned success, and committed nothing. A customer was told his transfer succeeded, but the money never moved, and we only found out when he called days later. The code looked correct and even passed shallow tests because the in-memory objects had the right values.

The fix is a matter of discipline. I only put readOnly true on genuine query methods, never on the class of a service that also writes. Read-only is something I add deliberately to a read method to get the optimization, not something I sprinkle across a class. If a class-level default must exist, I put an explicit writable @Transactional on every write method, because the method-level annotation always overrides the class-level one, which restores automatic flush so the writes actually persist.

The senior-level insight I always share is that readOnly true is a correctness switch disguised as a performance switch. On the read path it is great, because it lets Hibernate skip dirty checking and lets the infrastructure route queries to read replicas. On the write path it silently destroys data. So my rule is simple: prefer method-level annotations, mark only query methods readOnly, make every write method explicitly writable, and in code review treat any write happening under an inherited readOnly as a serious bug rather than a style issue.

answers.question: Describe a scenario where a @Transactional method rolled back but the API still returned HTTP 200 OK to the client. Why does this happen when a catch block swallows the exception and returns success? Why is this the most dangerous pitfall in transactional systems, and how do you fix it by aligning the HTTP status with the real transaction outcome using a PENDING to COMPLETED or FAILED state machine?
answers.shortTitle: Transaction rolled back but API returned HTTP 200 — the swallowed-exception pitfall

s1_definition.profdef: This pitfall occurs when a transactional method fails and Spring rolls back the database changes, but the surrounding controller catches the exception, swallows it, and returns a success response such as HTTP 200 OK. The database correctly undoes the work, yet the client is told the operation succeeded. The two outcomes, the real database state and the reported API status, disagree. The fix is to make the HTTP status a faithful reflection of the transaction outcome by letting exceptions propagate to a central handler, returning a success status only after a confirmed commit, and modeling the operation with an explicit state machine that moves from PENDING to either COMPLETED or FAILED.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh asks the National Bank of India to transfer Rs.50,000 to Priya. Deep inside, the vault refuses the transfer because of a rule violation and correctly puts the money back, so nothing moved. But the clerk at the counter, instead of telling Rajesh the truth, hides the rejection slip and hands Rajesh a receipt that says "Success." Rajesh leaves believing the rent is paid. Weeks later, the landlord says no money arrived, the bank's own reconciliation finds the mismatch, and now there is a dispute, an angry customer, and an audit problem. The clerk who hid the rejection and printed a fake success receipt is the swallowed-exception bug.
s1_definition.oneliner: If the transaction rolled back, the API must never say 200 — the HTTP status has to tell the same truth as the database.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This pitfall occurs when a transactional method fails and Spring rolls back the database changes, but the surrounding controller catches the exception, swallows it, and returns a success response such as HTTP 200 OK. The database correctly undoes the work, yet the client is told the operation succeeded. The two outcomes, the real database state and the reported API status, disagree. The fix is to make the HTTP status a faithful reflection of the transaction outcome by letting exceptions propagate to a central handler, returning a success status only after a confirmed commit, and modeling the operation with an explicit state machine that moves from PENDING to either COMPLETED or FAILED.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh asks the National Bank of India to transfer Rs.50,000 to Priya. Deep inside, the vault refuses the transfer because of a rule violation and correctly puts the money back, so nothing moved. But the clerk at the counter, instead of telling Rajesh the truth, hides the rejection slip and hands Rajesh a receipt that says "Success." Rajesh leaves believing the rent is paid. Weeks later, the landlord says no money arrived, the bank's own reconciliation finds the mismatch, and now there is a dispute, an angry customer, and an audit problem. The clerk who hid the rejection and printed a fake success receipt is the swallowed-exception bug.

**One line to remember:** If the transaction rolled back, the API must never say 200 — the HTTP status has to tell the same truth as the database.

sections.s2_technical:
Spring's declarative transactions work through a proxy. When your `@Transactional` service method throws a runtime exception, the proxy catches it, rolls back the transaction, and re-throws the exception so the caller knows something went wrong. The database is now clean, as if nothing happened. The danger is entirely in what the caller does with that exception.

The classic bug looks like this: `try { transferService.transfer(from, to, amount); } catch (Exception e) { return ResponseEntity.ok("Transfer done"); }`. The catch block swallows the exception and returns HTTP 200. The transaction already rolled back inside the service, so the money did not move, but the client receives a success. This is worse than a plain crash, because a crash is visible and gets fixed, while a false success is invisible and silently corrupts trust in the system. In banking it leads to reconciliation breaks days later, where the ledger and the client's belief do not match and nobody knows why.

A subtle sibling of this bug is returning 200 while the exception is still in flight toward rollback. If the controller and service share the same transaction and you catch the exception in the controller, Spring may still mark the transaction rollback-only and throw `UnexpectedRollbackException` at commit, or your success response goes out while the data is being undone. Either way the status and the data disagree.

The first part of the fix is to stop swallowing. Let the exception propagate out of the controller and handle it in one place with `@RestControllerAdvice` and `@ExceptionHandler`, mapping each exception type to the correct HTTP status. For example: `@ExceptionHandler(InsufficientFundsException.class) public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handle(InsufficientFundsException ex) { return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY).body(new ErrorResponse("TRANSFER_FAILED", ex.getMessage())); }`. Now a rollback produces a 4xx or 5xx, never a 200.

The second part is to return success only after a confirmed commit, which is where a state machine earns its keep. You model the operation as a record with a status column that starts at PENDING. The transactional method does the money movement and, within the same transaction, sets the status to COMPLETED. If anything throws, the whole transaction including the status update rolls back, so it never reaches COMPLETED. The controller then reads the committed result and returns 200 only if the stored status is COMPLETED, otherwise it returns a failure status. For a truly robust design you can combine this with a `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)` so that the success response or the downstream notification is only triggered after the commit is real. A senior-level point is that the state machine also gives you idempotency and auditability: every attempt leaves a durable row showing whether it ended COMPLETED or FAILED, which is exactly what reconciliation needs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the transfer API wrapped the call to the transactional service in a try-catch that returned HTTP 200 in all cases, because an early developer wanted to "never show errors to the customer." When Rajesh tried to transfer Rs.9,999,999 that he did not have, the service threw, Spring rolled back, but the API returned 200 with the message "Transfer successful." This is exactly the swallowed-exception pitfall — the rollback was correct, but the response lied.

Problem 2 — Because the customer and the mobile app both trusted the 200, Rajesh believed his rent was paid. The money never left his account. Days later, during end-of-month reconciliation, the operations team found that the app had recorded thousands of "successful" transfers that had no matching ledger entries. Tracing each one was slow and painful. This is exactly why this is called the most dangerous pitfall: the failure is silent, delayed, and discovered far from its cause.

Problem 3 — The fix was twofold. First, stop swallowing: let exceptions reach a central handler that maps failures to proper HTTP status codes, so a rolled-back transfer returns a 422, never a 200. Second, introduce a transfer record with a status that starts at PENDING, is set to COMPLETED inside the same transaction as the money movement, and therefore rolls back to never-COMPLETED if anything fails. The API returns 200 only when the committed status is COMPLETED. This is exactly how you align the HTTP status with the true transaction outcome.

What the code will do. We model an `Account` with debit and credit and a `Transfer` record with a status that moves PENDING to COMPLETED or FAILED. A `BrokenTransferController` demonstrates the bug by swallowing the exception and returning success. A `TransferService` performs the transfer and sets the status to COMPLETED inside the transaction. A `SafeTransferController` lets exceptions propagate and returns 200 only when the committed status is COMPLETED, otherwise a failure status, with a central exception handler mapping the failure. The demo shows a successful transfer returning COMPLETED and a failing transfer correctly returning FAILED instead of a false success.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a failing transfer of Rs.9,999,999 through the broken controller, then a successful Rs.50,000 and a failing Rs.9,999,999 through the safe controller.

Step 1. The broken controller calls the service for Rs.9,999,999. The service creates a transfer record in PENDING, begins the transaction, and tries to debit Rajesh. Rajesh does not have the money, so it throws, the balances roll back, and the exception is re-thrown.

Step 2. The broken controller catches the exception and returns HTTP 200 with status SUCCESS. This is the lie. The database correctly shows no money moved, but the client is told the transfer succeeded. Nothing here reveals the mismatch, which is what makes it dangerous.

Step 3. The safe controller runs a successful transfer of Rs.50,000. The service creates a PENDING record, begins the transaction, debits Rajesh, credits Priya, and sets the record to COMPLETED inside the same transaction. The transaction commits, so both the new balances and the COMPLETED status are durable together.

Step 4. The safe controller reads the committed status, sees COMPLETED, and returns HTTP 200. Here the 200 is honest because it is backed by a committed COMPLETED record.

Step 5. The safe controller runs the failing transfer of Rs.9,999,999. The service throws, the balances roll back, and the record never reaches COMPLETED. The controller returns HTTP 422 with status FAILED. The status and the database now tell the same story, so reconciliation will never break. Final balances are Rajesh Rs.950,000 and Priya Rs.300,000 from the one real transfer.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This pitfall happens when a transactional method fails, Spring correctly rolls back the database, but the controller catches the exception, swallows it, and returns HTTP 200 OK anyway. The database and the API now tell different stories. The money did not move, yet the client is told it did. I consider this the most dangerous transactional pitfall precisely because it is silent. A crash is visible and gets fixed quickly, but a false success is invisible, and in banking it surfaces days later as a reconciliation break where the ledger and the customer's belief do not match and nobody can explain why.

In my project at the National Bank of India, the transfer API wrapped the service call in a try-catch that returned 200 in every case, because an early developer wanted to never show errors to the customer. When Rajesh tried to send Rs.9,999,999 he did not have, the service threw, Spring rolled back, and the API still returned success. Rajesh thought his rent was paid, the money never left, and our end-of-month reconciliation found thousands of successful responses with no matching ledger entries.

The fix has two parts. First, stop swallowing exceptions. I let them propagate out of the controller and handle them in one place with a RestControllerAdvice, mapping each exception type to the correct HTTP status, so a rolled-back transfer returns a 422 and never a 200. Second, I model the operation as an explicit state machine. The transfer record starts in PENDING, and the status is set to COMPLETED inside the very same transaction that moves the money. Because the status change shares the transaction, if the money movement rolls back the status never becomes COMPLETED. The controller then returns 200 only when the committed status is COMPLETED, otherwise it returns a failure status.

The senior-level insight I always add is that the HTTP status must be a faithful mirror of the committed transaction outcome, not a hopeful guess made before the commit. Binding success to a committed COMPLETED state, and in the most robust designs firing the success notification only from an after-commit event listener, means the client, the database, and the downstream systems can never disagree. As a bonus, the PENDING to COMPLETED or FAILED state machine gives me idempotency and a durable audit trail, which is exactly what reconciliation needs, so the whole class of silent false-success bugs simply cannot occur.
